narrative:
The model estimated a 63.9% chance that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt, meaning that among applicants with a similar profile, roughly 64 in 100 were predicted to fail. Because the model classified you as likely to fail, your law school application was denied. This is a risk estimate, not a certainty about your ability.

The denial was driven mainly by your class-standing profile. Your third-year class-standing decile was the strongest factor: at 1, it places you near the bottom of your class and is far below the accepted average of 5.79. That pushed the prediction strongly toward bar-exam failure. Your first-year decile was the second most influential factor; at 2, it is also well below the accepted average of 6.00 and pushed in the same unfavorable direction. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor. Although your 2.40 is below the accepted average of 3.23, this factor’s influence worked in your favor, pushing toward passing rather than failure.

To improve a future application, focus on the areas treated as strongest: seek academic advising and a plan to raise your class standing or demonstrate stronger advanced coursework, and consider post-baccalaureate or graduate study if needed. Ask admissions for feedback, retake the LSAT if practice scores suggest meaningful improvement, and apply to programs that review applicants holistically. Use the estimate as a signal to address academic readiness, not as a final verdict.
